title: The lilies of the field (Matthew 6:28–34)
hookLine: consider the lilies; don't worry about tomorrow, today has enough

cards: A lot of time goes into what you wear. The morning in front of the mirror. The shirt that's fine but not quite right.

The outfit for the interview, the wedding, the first date. Clothes say who you are, or who you're afraid you aren't. In Jesus's world, every thread was spun and woven by hand; the passage itself mentions the spinning.
So when he moves from food to clothes, he's touching a real fear. And again he doesn't argue. He crouches down, so to speak, and points at the ground.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin: And yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these."
Consider is a careful word. The Greek means to learn something thoroughly, to study it until you understand. So: really look at a flower.
Which flower? Nobody knows. The word is general, and some readers think Jesus meant the wildflowers that cover Galilee's hills in spring, whatever grew at his feet that day.

Then Solomon, the king Israel remembered for his glory, outdressed by a wild flower. The next line is sharper: the grass is here today and tomorrow it's thrown in the oven. Dried grass went into the oven as fuel.
Beautiful and brief. If God dresses something that brief so lavishly, the reasoning goes, how much more you.
Then the order of things: "But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you." First. Not only.
Food and clothes still matter; they just aren't the center.

And a blunt ending: "Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof." It doesn't promise that today will be easy.
It says today has enough trouble of its own. Don't borrow tomorrow's too. One day's load at a time.

how: Some Christians read Matthew 6:34 in hard seasons and try to live one day at a time, and some keep a flower or a plant in view as a small reminder of the passage.

o: a disciple who left his riches to follow Jesus
a prophet who wrote the Psalms in the desert
the king remembered for glory, outdressed by a flower

games.q: what's in the passage — tap the pairs.

s: we know exactly which flower Jesus meant
the word is general. some readers think he meant Galilee's spring wildflowers.
Jesus promises that today will be easy
"Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof." today has enough trouble; don't add tomorrow's.
the Greek is a learning word: look until you understand.

games.q: you're worried about what to wear and what to eat. Jesus doesn't say those don't matter. what does he say to do with them?
o: seek the kingdom first, and let these come after.
games.why: "But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you." first, not only.

practice: Lean in close to a flower near you, a plant on the sill, a weed by the door, or picture one you know well: the edges of the petals, the color where it changes, the center. Nobody sewed that.
Let these minutes be only today, and if tomorrow's list starts talking, tell it: tomorrow will take care of itself.

wordCard.voice: Solomon, the king remembered for his glory, whom Jesus says a wildflower outdresses. Here today, gone tomorrow, and dressed anyway.

orig.note: Greek: consider, learn thoroughly; from the verb for learning.

carryVoice: Your line: today is enough. Tomorrow's trouble can wait for tomorrow. That's day two hundred fifty-four.
